Densify COMPLETE (mid PHYS 339–mid-345): Cap. 2 title; immortality shown by nature and Scripture (Alsted); Gentile barbarians and philosophers; ancient Getae and Egyptians (Herodotus, Diodorus); recently discovered peoples and antipodes digression (Lactantius, Augustine, Besoldus); Guineans, Chinese, Peruvians (Acosta), Mexicans, Guianans (Raleigh), Tupinamba (Lery), Virginians (Hariot); what barbarian confession shows — Cap. 2 close. source_text: CAPUT SECUNDUM, De animae immortalitate, ex luce naturae & confessione barbarorum, tum veterum, tum patrum nostra memoria detectorum. Animam vero nostram rationalem ab interitu liberam post suum a corpore discessum superesse, luce naturae & scripturae, tanquam ad duas faculas in obscuro lucentes, ostenditur. Vide Alstedii nostri Encyclopaediae lib. 6, pneumatica parte 4. cap. 2.
english: CHAPTER TWO. On the immortality of the soul, from the light of nature and the confession of barbarians, both the ancient and those discovered in our own memory.

That our rational soul, free from destruction, survives after its departure from the body is shown by the light of nature and of Scripture, as by two torches shining in the dark. See our Alsted's Encyclopaedia, book 6, pneumatic part 4, chapter 2.

source_text: XIII. Hac barbarorum confessio ostendit, 1. Quod de immortalitate animae & hujus post obitum beatitate aut miseria constans ubique gentium sit sententia, e principiis naturae, de quibus in pneumatologia, hausta, quae videri possit non tam addisci quam connasci. Omni enim in re consensus omnium gentium lex naturae putanda est, authore Cicerone 1. Tusc. de quo communi consensu etiam fidem faciunt opiniones vulgares gentilium sive fabulae de manibus, campis Elysiis, tartaro a poetis, Homero Odys. λ. Virgilio Aeneid. 6. & Ovidio 2. Fast. decantatae, quae immortalitatem animae tanquam fundamentum, ex quo natae sunt, & sine quo nasci non potuissent, subiternunt. 2. Quod iis, quae vera quidem sunt, e lumine naturae legitime deducta, gentium tenebrae superstruxerint falsa, vana, impia. Verum est, animas esse immortales, iisque post suum a corpore discessum bene fore aut male. Falsum est, felicitatem ob victoriam ab externis hostibus reportatam obvenire. Vanum est, supellectilem quasi in altero orbe sui futuram contumulari. Impium vero etiam est & plus quam superstitiosum, homines eo fine trucidare, ut defunctorum in aeterna vita commodis prospiciatur.
english: XIII. This confession of the barbarians shows: 1. That concerning the immortality of the soul and its beatitude or misery after death there is a constant opinion among all nations, drawn from the principles of nature (of which see in pneumatology), which may seem not so much learned as connate. For in every matter the consensus of all nations is to be counted the law of nature, as Cicero authorizes in Tusculan Disputations book 1; of which common consensus the vulgar opinions of the Gentiles, or the fables of shades, the Elysian fields, and Tartarus sung by the poets — Homer in Odyssey book 11, Virgil in Aeneid 6, and Ovid in Fasti book 2 — also give faith, which rest upon the immortality of the soul as a foundation from which they were born and without which they could not have been born.

2. That upon those things which are indeed true and legitimately deduced from the light of nature, the darknesses of the nations have built false, vain, and impious additions. It is true that souls are immortal, and that after their departure from the body it will go well or ill with them. It is false that happiness comes on account of victory won over external enemies. It is vain that household goods should be buried as if they would be of use in another world. And it is also impious and more than superstitious to slaughter human beings to that end, that provision may be made for the comforts of the dead in eternal life.

source_text: XI. TououPINAMBAULTII, Brasilenses, feri & anthropophagi, immortalitatem animarum credunt. Nam de his Johannes Lerius annum inter eos versatus cap. 16. scribit, se non credere, gentem ullam in toto terrarum orbe esse, quae ab omni religione sit magis aliena: si tamen, ipso teste, non modo immortalitatem animarum credebant, sed pro certo quoque habebant, post mortem eorum animas, qui virtutem coluerint (Virtutem autem illi definiunt suo more, nempe ultionem sumere de hostibus, & quam plurimos devorare) post altissimos montes evolantes patrum & avorum suorum animis aggregari, ibique in amoenissimis hortis perpetuis deliciis ac tripudiis laetum aevum agere: ignavorum contra manes, qui sine ulla propugnandae patriae cura inglorii vixerint, abripi ad Aygnan (sic cacodaemonem vocant) & cum eo sempiternos inter cruciatus vivere.
english: XI. THE TUPINAMBA, Brazilians, fierce and cannibals, believe the immortality of souls. For concerning them Jean de Lery, who spent a year among them, writes in chapter 16 that he does not believe there is any nation in the whole globe of lands more alien from all religion: if nevertheless, by his own witness, they not only believed the immortality of souls, but also held it for certain that after death the souls of those who had cultivated virtue (but they define virtue in their own way — namely to take vengeance on enemies and to devour as many as possible), flying past the highest mountains, are gathered to the souls of their fathers and grandfathers, and there in most pleasant gardens spend a joyful age in perpetual delights and dances: but on the contrary the shades of the cowardly, who have lived without any care of defending the fatherland and ingloriously, are snatched away to Aygnan (so they call the evil demon) and live with him amid everlasting torments.

source_text: VII. CHINENSES, quorum religio, sine Mahumedismi contagione, mere pagana, credunt omnes immortalitatem animae, atque post hanc vitam retributionem bonorum malorumve, prout quisque bona malave gesserit, & ob id monumenta sepulchralia magnifice excisa defunctis statuunt. Credunt in altero mundo vitam immortalem esse, teste Hugone Linscotano part. 1. cap. 25.
english: VII. THE CHINESE, whose religion — without the contagion of Mohammedanism — is merely pagan, all believe the immortality of the soul, and after this life a retribution of goods or evils according as each has done good or evil things, and on that account they set up for the dead sepulchral monuments magnificently carved. They believe there is an immortal life in the other world, as Hugo Linschoten witnesses, part 1, chapter 25.

source_text: VIII. PERUANI animae immortalitatem & vitam, mortemque aeternam credunt. Josephus Acosta lib. 5. cap. 7. Indi, inquit, qui in Peru habitant, statuunt animas hominum immortales esse, ac pios vitam aeternam, impios autem aeternam damnationem manere. Ideoque ad hujus articuli fidem suscipiendam adduci facile possunt. Corpora vero una cum ipsis animabus aliquando resurrectura esse, omnino ignorabant. Atque hinc scribit factum esse, ut de altera vita soliciti mancipia in exequiis suorum mactarent, quae ibi ministrarent. Confer Hieronymum Benzonem historiae novi orbis lib. 3. cap. 20.
english: VIII. THE PERUVIANS believe the immortality of the soul and eternal life and death. Joseph Acosta, book 5, chapter 7: The Indians who dwell in Peru, he says, hold that the souls of men are immortal, and that eternal life awaits the pious, but eternal damnation the impious. And therefore they can easily be led to take up the faith of this article. But that bodies would one day rise again together with the souls themselves they were wholly ignorant. And from this he writes that it came about that, anxious about the other life, they slaughtered slaves at the funerals of their own, to minister there. Compare Girolamo Benzoni, History of the New World book 3, chapter 20.
